title: How a Robin Builds a Nest

p: A robin needs a safe place to lay her eggs.
She finds a strong fork where a tree branch splits in two.
She brings grass and small twigs to the fork, one piece at a time.
She packs wet mud inside the bowl and presses it down with her chest.
The mud dries hard and holds the whole nest together.
A robin needs a safe place for her eggs.
She finds a fork in a tree branch.
She brings grass and twigs to the fork.
She packs wet mud inside the nest.
The mud dries hard and holds it together.

qs: main idea/detail
Where does the robin build her nest?
She finds a strong fork where a tree branch splits in two.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. grass and twigs) and paragraph D (i.e. the wet mud).
summarize
Tell how a robin builds a nest.
She finds a fork in a tree branch, brings grass and twigs one piece at a time, packs wet mud inside, and the mud dries hard and holds the nest together.
vocabulary

fork: the place where a branch splits in two.
twig: a very small, thin stick.
connection
Describe the connection between the mud and the nest staying together.
She packs wet mud inside the bowl, and the mud dries hard and holds the whole nest together.
note: RI.1.1 is asking and answering from details, so every answer is printed. Have the child put a finger on the sentence before saying it out loud.

title: What a Frog Catches

p: A frog sits very still at the edge of the pond.
It waits for a bug to fly close enough.
A frog's tongue is long, pink and very sticky.
The tongue snaps out and grabs the bug in a flash.
The whole catch takes less than one second to finish.
A frog sits still at the pond.
It waits for a bug to come close.
Its tongue is long and sticky.
The tongue snaps out and grabs the bug.
The whole catch is very fast.

qs: main idea/detail
What is a frog's tongue like?
A frog's tongue is long, pink and very sticky.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. waiting) and paragraph D (i.e. the catch).
summarize
Tell how a frog catches a bug.
It sits very still at the edge of the pond and waits for a bug to come close. Then its long sticky tongue snaps out and grabs the bug in less than one second.
vocabulary

sticky: able to hold on to things that touch it.
snaps: moves out very fast and then back again.
connection
Describe the connection between sitting still and catching a bug.
The frog sits very still and waits for a bug to fly close enough, so the bug comes near without being scared away.
note: Paragraph A and paragraph B are both about waiting. Ask why the writer gave waiting two paragraphs when the catch only gets one.

title: The Crossing Guard

p: A crossing guard stands at the corner by the school.
She wears a bright vest so every driver can see her.
She holds up a round sign that tells cars to stop.
When the cars stop, she waves the children across the street.
She stays in the road until the last child is safe.
A crossing guard stands by the school.
She wears a bright vest so drivers see her.
She holds up a sign that says stop.
Then she waves the children across.
She waits until every child is safe.

qs: main idea/detail
Why does the crossing guard wear a bright vest?
She wears a bright vest so every driver can see her.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the stop sign) and paragraph E (i.e. staying until the end).
summarize
Tell what a crossing guard does.
She stands at the corner by the school in a bright vest, holds up a sign that tells cars to stop, waves the children across, and stays in the road until the last child is safe.
vocabulary

vest: a bright coat with no sleeves, worn so people can see you.
guard: a person whose job is keeping others safe.
connection
Describe the connection between the sign and the children crossing.
She holds up a round sign that tells cars to stop, and when the cars stop she waves the children across the street.
note: The order is the lesson here: sign first, then cars stop, then children cross. Ask what would happen if those swapped.

title: Why a Cat Purrs

p: A cat purrs by shaking the muscles in its throat very fast.
The shake happens when the cat breathes in and when it breathes out.
That is why a purr does not stop between breaths.
Most cats purr when they feel safe and warm.
Some cats also purr when they are hurt or scared.
A cat purrs with the muscles in its throat.
The shake happens when it breathes in and out.
So a purr does not stop between breaths.
Most cats purr when they feel safe.
Some purr when they are hurt or scared.

qs: main idea/detail
What part of a cat makes the purr?
A cat purrs by shaking the muscles in its throat very fast.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. why a purr never stops) and paragraph E (i.e. purring when hurt).
summarize
Tell how and why a cat purrs.

A cat shakes the muscles in its throat very fast, both breathing in and breathing out, so the purr never stops between breaths. Most cats purr when they feel safe, and some purr when they are hurt or scared.
vocabulary

muscle: a part inside the body that can pull and move.
purr: the soft rumbling sound a cat makes.
connection
Describe the connection between breathing and the sound of a purr.
The shake happens when the cat breathes in and when it breathes out, which is why a purr does not stop between breaths.
note: Paragraph E is the surprise and children will want to talk about it. The text says some cats purr when hurt; it does not say why, and that is worth admitting.

title: The Mail Carrier's Bag

p: A mail carrier sorts the mail into streets before she leaves.
Each street goes in order, so the first house comes first.
Her bag is heavy at the start and light at the end.
She walks the same route every day and knows every dog.
The letters at the bottom of the bag are the last stop.
A mail carrier sorts the mail into streets.
Each street is in order, so the first house is first.
Her bag is heavy at the start.
She walks the same route every day.
The mail at the bottom is the last stop.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the mail carrier do before she leaves?
She sorts the mail into streets before she leaves.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the order) and paragraph E (i.e. the bottom of the bag).
summarize
Tell how a mail carrier gets the mail to the right houses.

She sorts the mail into streets before she leaves, puts each street in order so the first house comes first, and walks the same route every day. The letters at the bottom of the bag are the last stop.
vocabulary

sort: to put things into groups that belong together.
route: the same path a person takes each day.
connection
Describe the connection between sorting the mail and the bag getting lighter.
Each street goes in order so the first house comes first, which is why her bag is heavy at the start and light at the end.
note: Children often miss that the bottom of the bag is the end of the route. It follows from paragraph B, so read those two together.

title: Bees and Flowers

p: A bee lands on a flower to drink the sweet nectar.
Yellow dust called pollen sticks to the hairs on her legs.
She flies to the next flower and some pollen rubs off.
That pollen helps the flower make seeds.
Bees get food and flowers get seeds, so both of them win.
A bee lands on a flower to drink.
Yellow pollen sticks to her legs.
She flies to the next flower.
Some pollen rubs off and helps make seeds.
Bees get food and flowers get seeds.

qs: main idea/detail
What sticks to the bee's legs?
Yellow dust called pollen sticks to the hairs on her legs.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the next flower) and paragraph E (i.e. both of them win).
summarize
Tell the main topic of this text.
Bees and flowers help each other. A bee drinks nectar and pollen sticks to her legs. She rubs some off on the next flower, and that pollen helps the flower make seeds.
vocabulary

nectar: the sweet juice inside a flower.
pollen: the yellow dust a flower makes.
connection
Describe the connection between the bee's legs and the flower's seeds.
Pollen sticks to the hairs on her legs, and when she flies to the next flower some pollen rubs off and helps that flower make seeds.
note: The main topic is the trade, not the bee. Ask what the last paragraph adds that the first four do not.

title: The Fire Station

p: The fire station is open all day and all night.
The truck is backed in so it can drive straight out.
Boots and coats wait by the truck with the pants already open.
A firefighter can step in and pull them up in seconds.
Every second saved is a second sooner at the fire.
The fire station is open all night.
The truck is backed in so it can drive out.
Boots and coats wait by the truck.
A firefighter can step in fast.

qs: main idea/detail
Why is the truck backed in?
The truck is backed in so it can drive straight out.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the waiting boots) and paragraph E (i.e. seconds saved).
summarize
Tell the main topic of this text.
A fire station is set up so firefighters can leave fast. The truck is backed in, the boots and coats wait by the truck with the pants open, and a firefighter can step in and pull them up in seconds.
vocabulary

station: the building where fire trucks and firefighters stay.
second: a very short piece of time.
connection
Describe the connection between the open pants and getting to the fire.
The pants are already open so a firefighter can step in and pull them up in seconds, and every second saved is a second sooner at the fire.
note: Everything here is one idea in five parts: be fast. Ask the child to say the idea in their own words before retelling the details.

title: How Rain Falls

p: The sun warms a puddle and the water turns into vapor.
The vapor rises up into the cold air above.
Up high it cools and sticks to tiny bits of dust.
Many drops join together until they are too heavy to float.
Then they fall back down as rain.
The sun warms a puddle and the water rises.
The vapor goes up into cold air.
Up high it cools into tiny drops.
Drops join until they are too heavy.

qs: main idea/detail
What makes the drops fall?
Many drops join together until they are too heavy to float.
paragraph focus
Paragraph A (i.e. the sun and the puddle) and paragraph D (i.e. the drops joining).
summarize
Tell the main topic of this text.
Water goes up and comes back down. The sun turns a puddle into vapor, the vapor rises into cold air and cools onto bits of dust, and the drops join until they are heavy enough to fall as rain.
vocabulary

vapor: water that has turned into air you cannot see.
float: to stay up without falling.
connection
Describe the connection between the sun and the rain.
The sun warms a puddle and the water turns into vapor, and that vapor is what rises, cools and falls back down as rain.
note: This is a circle and the text does not say so. Ask where the rain goes next, and whether paragraph A could come after paragraph E.

title: The Library Card

p: A library card has your name and a long number on it.
The number tells the computer which books you took home.
You may keep a book for three weeks.
A card is free, and the books you borrow are free too.
When you bring a book back, someone else can read it.
A library card has your name and a number.
The number tells the computer what you took.
You may keep a book for three weeks.
The card is free and the books are free.
When you bring it back, someone else can read it.

qs: main idea/detail
How long may you keep a book?
You may keep a book for three weeks.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the number) and paragraph E (i.e. bringing a book back).
summarize
Tell the main topic of this text.

A library card lets you borrow books for free. It has your name and a number that tells the computer which books you took, you may keep a book for three weeks, and when you bring it back someone else can read it.
vocabulary

borrow: to take something for a while and then give it back.
free: costing no money.
connection
Describe the connection between bringing a book back and other readers.
When you bring a book back, someone else can read it.
note: Paragraph E is the point of the whole system and it comes last. Ask why the writer saved it for the end.

title: A Seed Grows

p: A seed holds a tiny plant and a packed lunch for it.
Water makes the hard coat swell until it cracks open.
A root goes down first, before anything goes up.
Then a green shoot pushes up toward the light.
Once the first leaves open, the plant can make its own food.
A seed holds a tiny plant and its food.
Water makes the hard coat crack open.
Then a green shoot pushes up.
When leaves open, the plant makes its own food.

qs: main idea/detail
What goes out of the seed first?
A root goes down first, before anything goes up.
paragraph focus
Paragraph A (i.e. the packed lunch) and paragraph E (i.e. making its own food).
summarize
Tell the main topic of this text.
A seed grows in order. It holds a tiny plant and food for it, water cracks the coat open, a root goes down first, a shoot pushes up, and once the leaves open the plant makes its own food.
vocabulary

root: the part of a plant that grows down into the soil.
shoot: the new green stem that pushes up.
connection
Describe the connection between the packed lunch and the first leaves.
A seed holds a packed lunch for the tiny plant, and once the first leaves open the plant can make its own food instead.
note: Paragraph A and paragraph E are a pair: food that came with the seed, then food the plant makes. The three middle paragraphs sit between them in order.

title: The Sun and the Puddle

p: On Monday the rain left a big puddle on the path.
By Tuesday the sun was out all morning.
By lunch the puddle was only a damp ring.
The sun turned the water into a vapor you cannot see.
But a puddle in the shade was still there on Wednesday.
Rain left a big puddle on the path.
The sun came out all morning.
By lunch the puddle was small.
The sun turned the water into vapor.
A puddle in the shade was still there.

qs: main idea/detail
What happened to the puddle in the shade?
A puddle in the shade was still there on Wednesday.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the sun) and paragraph E (i.e. the shade).
summarize
Tell what this text is about.
The sun dried a puddle. Rain left a big puddle, the sun was out all morning, and by lunch it was only a damp ring. A puddle in the shade was still there the next day.
vocabulary

damp: a little bit wet.
shade: a place the sun does not reach.
connection
Describe the connection between the sun and the puddle drying.
The sun was out all morning and turned the water into vapor you cannot see, so by lunch the puddle was only a damp ring.
note: The shade puddle is the proof and it comes last. Ask the child what it shows that paragraphs A to D do not.

title: The Bell and the Line

p: The bell rings at the end of recess every day.
When it rings, the children stop playing and walk to the line.
The line forms on the yellow paint by the door.
A teacher counts the children before the line goes in.
The bell is the start of all of it.
The bell rings at the end of recess.
The children stop playing and walk to the line.
The line forms on the yellow paint.
The bell starts all of it.

qs: main idea/detail
Where does the line form?
The line forms on the yellow paint by the door.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. walking to the line) and paragraph D (i.e. the counting).
summarize
Tell what happens after the bell rings.
The bell rings at the end of recess, the children stop playing and walk to the line on the yellow paint, and a teacher counts them before the line goes in.
vocabulary

recess: the time outside for playing.
form: to come together into a shape, like a line.
connection
Describe the connection between the bell and the children lining up.
When the bell rings, the children stop playing and walk to the line, so the bell is the start of all of it.
note: Paragraph E names the connection outright. Cover it and see whether the child can say it before reading it.

title: Why the Beach Changes

p: Early in the morning the beach is wide and flat.
By afternoon the water has come far up the sand.
The moon pulls on the ocean as the Earth turns.
That pull makes the water rise and fall twice every day.
The wide beach comes back again by night.
In the morning the beach is wide.
By afternoon the water comes up the sand.
The moon pulls on the ocean.
The water rises and falls twice a day.
The wide beach comes back by night.

qs: main idea/detail
How many times a day does the water rise and fall?
That pull makes the water rise and fall twice a day.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the moon) and paragraph E (i.e. night).
summarize
Tell why the beach changes.
The moon pulls on the ocean as the Earth turns, and that pull makes the water rise and fall twice a day. So a beach that is wide in the morning is covered by afternoon and wide again by night.
vocabulary

pull: to draw something toward you.
ocean: the very large body of salt water.
connection
Describe the connection between the moon and the water on the sand.
The moon pulls on the ocean as the Earth turns, and that pull makes the water rise and fall twice a day.
note: The cause is invisible and far away, which is hard at this age. Keep the child on what they can see in paragraphs A, B and E first.

title: The Farmer and the Market

p: A farmer picks beans early, while the air is still cool.
Cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones do.
She packs them in boxes and drives to the market.
By eight o'clock her table is full and the doors open.
Beans picked the day before would already be soft.
A farmer picks beans early while it is cool.
Cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones.
She packs them and drives to the market.
By eight her table is full.

qs: main idea/detail
Why does the farmer pick beans early?
Cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones do.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. why cool matters) and paragraph E (i.e. older beans).
summarize
Tell why the farmer picks early.
She picks beans early while the air is still cool, because cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones. She packs them and drives to the market, and by eight o'clock her table is full.
vocabulary

crisp: firm and fresh, so it snaps.
market: a place where people sell food.
connection
Describe the connection between the cool morning air and the beans on the table.
She picks beans early while the air is still cool, because cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones do.
note: Paragraph E is the comparison that makes the reason land. Read B and E together.

title: The Fly and the Web

p: A spider's web has sticky threads and plain ones mixed together.
The spider walks only on the plain threads, so it never sticks.
A fly cannot tell the two kinds apart.
When a fly hits a sticky thread, the whole web shakes.
The spider feels the shake and knows just where to go.
A web has sticky threads and plain ones.
The spider walks only on the plain ones.
A fly cannot tell them apart.
When a fly hits a sticky thread, the web shakes.
The spider feels the shake and goes there.

qs: main idea/detail
Why does the spider not stick to its own web?
The spider walks only on the plain threads, so it never sticks.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the fly not knowing) and paragraph D (i.e. the shake).
summarize
Tell how a spider knows a fly is caught.

A web has sticky threads and plain ones mixed together, and the spider walks only on the plain ones. A fly cannot tell them apart, so when it hits a sticky thread the whole web shakes and the spider feels it.
vocabulary

thread: one thin line of a web.
plain: not sticky, just ordinary.
connection
Describe the connection between the shaking web and the spider finding the fly.
When a fly hits a sticky thread the whole web shakes, and the spider feels the shake and knows just where to go.
note: Two connections sit in this text: why the spider is safe, and how it gets the news. Ask the child for both.

title: What Hibernate Means

p: The book says the bear will hibernate all winter long.
Hibernate is a word for a long, deep winter sleep.
A bear that hibernates does not eat for many months.
Its heart beats slower and its body stays cool.
In spring the bear wakes up thin and very hungry.
The book says the bear will hibernate all winter.
Hibernate means a long, deep winter sleep.
The bear does not eat for months.
Its heart beats slower and it stays cool.
In spring it wakes up hungry.

qs: main idea/detail
What does hibernate mean?
Hibernate is a word for a long, deep winter sleep.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. what the word means) and paragraph E (i.e. waking up).
summarize
Tell what hibernate means and what a bear does.
Hibernate means a long, deep winter sleep. A bear that hibernates does not eat for many months, its heart beats slower and its body stays cool, and in spring it wakes up thin and very hungry.
vocabulary

hibernate: to sleep deeply all winter.
spring: the season that comes after winter.
connection
Describe the connection between not eating and waking up thin.
A bear that hibernates does not eat for many months, so in spring it wakes up thin and very hungry.
note: RI.1.4 is asking about a word, so paragraph B is the answer and the rest is evidence. Ask the child which paragraph gives them the meaning.

title: Words That Tell Where

p: A map uses small words to tell you where to go.
Above means higher up, and below means lower down.
Beside means right next to something else on the map.
Between means in the middle of two other things.
If you miss those small words, the map cannot help you.
A map uses small words to tell where.
Above means higher. Below means lower.
Between means in the middle of two things.
If you miss them, the map will not help.

qs: main idea/detail
What does between mean?
Between means in the middle of two other things.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. above and below) and paragraph E (i.e. missing the words).
summarize
Tell what this text teaches.

A map uses small words to tell you where to go. Above means higher up and below means lower down, beside means right next to, and between means in the middle of two things. If you miss those words the map cannot help you.
vocabulary

beside: right next to something.
between: in the middle of two things.
connection
Describe the connection between the small words and using a map.
A map uses small words to tell you where to go, so if you miss those small words the map cannot help you.
note: These are the words that trip children up on every map all year. Have them put a finger on two things and say what is between them.

title: What Melt Means

p: Melt means to change from hard into something soft and runny.
Ice melts into plain water when it gets warm enough.
Butter melts in a hot pan and spreads out flat.
A crayon left on a sunny sill can melt too.
Heat is what makes all of those things melt.
Melt means to change from hard to runny.
Ice melts into water when it is warm.
Butter melts in a hot pan.
A crayon in the sun can melt.
Heat makes all of them melt.

qs: main idea/detail
What does melt mean?
Melt means to change from hard into something soft and runny.
paragraph focus
Paragraph A (i.e. the meaning) and paragraph E (i.e. what they all share).
summarize
Tell what melt means and give examples.
Melt means to change from hard into something soft and runny. Ice melts into water, butter melts in a hot pan, and a crayon on a sunny sill can melt. Heat is what makes all of those things melt.
vocabulary

melt: to change from hard into soft and runny.
heat: warmth that can change things.
connection
Describe the connection between the three examples in the middle.
Ice, butter and a crayon are all different, and heat is what makes all of those things melt.
note: The shape is a definition, three examples and the thing they share. Ask what all three have in common before reading paragraph E.

title: Signs at the Pool

p: A sign at the pool says NO DIVING in big letters.
Diving means going in head first instead of feet first.
Another sign says to WALK and not to run.
A third sign tells you how deep the water is.
Reading those signs before you swim keeps you safe.
A sign at the pool says NO DIVING.
Diving means going in head first.
Another sign says to walk, not run.
A third sign tells how deep the water is.
Read the signs to stay safe.

qs: main idea/detail
What does diving mean?
Diving means going in head first instead of feet first.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. what diving means) and paragraph D (i.e. the depth sign).
summarize
Tell what the signs at the pool say.
One sign says NO DIVING, which means going in head first. Another says to walk and not run, and a third tells you how deep the water is. Reading those signs before you swim keeps you safe.
vocabulary

diving: going into water head first.
deep: going far down from the top.
connection
Describe the connection between reading the signs and staying safe.
Reading those signs before you swim keeps you safe.
note: The word children get wrong is diving, because they use it for any jump. Paragraph B is there for exactly that.

title: Float and Sink

p: Float means to stay up on top of the water.
Sink means to go all the way down to the bottom.
A cork floats, and a small rock sinks.
A big boat floats even though it is very heavy.
So what matters is not just weight but shape too.
Float means to stay on top of the water.
Sink means to go down to the bottom.
A cork floats and a rock sinks.
A big boat floats, and it is heavy.
So weight is not the only thing.

qs: main idea/detail
What does sink mean?
Sink means to go all the way down to the bottom.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the cork and the rock) and paragraph D (i.e. the boat).
summarize
Tell what float and sink mean.

Float means to stay up on top of the water and sink means to go down to the bottom. A cork floats and a small rock sinks, but a big heavy boat floats too, so what matters is not just weight but shape.
vocabulary

float: to stay up on top of water.
sink: to go down to the bottom.
connection
Describe the connection between the boat and the rest of the text.
A cork floats and a small rock sinks, but a big boat floats even though it is very heavy, so what matters is not just weight but shape too.
note: Paragraph D breaks the rule paragraph C sets up, and that is deliberate. Ask the child why a heavy boat does not sink.

title: The List at the Front

p: The first page of this book is a list.
The list shows every part of the book in order.
Next to each part is the page it starts on.
If you want frogs, the list sends you to page nine.
You do not have to turn every page to find it.
The first page of this book is a list.
It shows every part in order.
Each part has a page number.
If you want frogs, go to page nine.
You do not turn every page.

qs: main idea/detail
What is next to each part on the list?
Next to each part is the page it starts on.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. finding frogs) and paragraph E (i.e. not turning every page).
summarize
Tell what the list at the front is for.
The first page is a list that shows every part of the book in order, with the page each part starts on. If you want frogs the list sends you to page nine, so you do not have to turn every page.
vocabulary

list: names written one under another.
page number: the number that tells you which page you are on.
connection
Describe the connection between the list and finding what you want.
Next to each part is the page it starts on, so the list sends you straight to page nine instead of turning every page.
note: This is a table of contents and the text never uses the term. Name it after the child has used it, not before.

title: The Word List at the Back

p: At the back of the book there is a word list.
It holds the hard words from every page.
The words are in ABC order, so they are easy to find.
After each word is a short line that tells what it means.
You can look up a word without asking anyone.
At the back of the book is a word list.
The words are in ABC order.
After each word is what it means.
You can look up a word by yourself.

qs: main idea/detail
What order are the words in?
The words are in ABC order, so they are easy to find.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. ABC order) and paragraph E (i.e. looking it up yourself).
summarize
Tell what the word list at the back is for.
The back of the book has a list of the hard words from every page, in ABC order, with a short line after each one telling what it means. You can look up a word without asking anyone.
vocabulary

ABC order: the order of the letters of the alphabet.
means: what a word is telling you.
connection
Describe the connection between ABC order and finding a word fast.
The words are in ABC order, so they are easy to find and you can look one up without asking anyone.
note: This is a glossary. Point out that it only holds words from this book, which is what makes it different from a dictionary.

title: Headings Tell You Where

p: A heading is the dark line above a part of a page.
It says in a few words what that part is about.
A heading that says Eggs tells you eggs come next.
You can read just the headings to find what you need.
Headings save you from reading the whole page.
A heading is the dark line above a part.
It tells what that part is about.
A heading that says Eggs means eggs come next.
You can read just the headings.
Headings save you reading the whole page.

qs: main idea/detail
What does a heading tell you?
It says in a few words what that part is about.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the Eggs heading) and paragraph E (i.e. saving reading).
summarize
Tell what headings do.

A heading is the dark line above a part of a page, and it says in a few words what that part is about. A heading that says Eggs tells you eggs come next, so you can read just the headings to find what you need.
vocabulary

heading: the dark line of words above a part of a page.
about: what something is telling you.
connection
Describe the connection between reading headings and reading the whole page.
You can read just the headings to find what you need, which saves you from reading the whole page.
note: Have the child find a heading in any book on the shelf and say what will come under it before they read it.

title: Buttons You Can Tap

p: A screen has small pictures you can tap with a finger.
A tiny house always takes you back to the start.
A round glass means you can search for something.
An arrow that curls back means undo what you just did.
The pictures mean the same thing on almost every screen.
A screen has small pictures you can tap.
A tiny house takes you back to the start.
A round glass means you can search.
The pictures mean the same on most screens.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the tiny house do?
A tiny house always takes you back to the start.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. the curling arrow) and paragraph E (i.e. every screen).
summarize
Tell what the small pictures on a screen do.

A screen has small pictures you tap with a finger. A tiny house takes you back to the start, a round glass means search, and an arrow that curls back means undo. They mean the same thing on almost every screen.
vocabulary

tap: to touch a screen once with a finger.
undo: to take back what you just did.
connection
Describe the connection between learning these pictures and using a new screen.
The pictures mean the same thing on almost every screen, so learning them once helps on a screen you have never used.
note: Paragraph E is the useful part and children will skip it for the pictures. It is why learning three icons is worth the time.

title: The Numbers at the Bottom

p: Look at the very bottom corner of this page.
A small number sits there, and the next page is one more.
Page numbers let a list at the front point at a page.
They also let you stop reading and find your place again.
A book with no page numbers is hard to talk about.
Look at the bottom corner of the page.
The next page is one more.
Numbers help you find your place again.
They also let the list point at a page.

qs: main idea/detail
Where do you find the page number?
Look at the very bottom corner of this page.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. pointing from the list) and paragraph D (i.e. finding your place).
summarize
Tell what page numbers are for.
A small number sits at the bottom corner of each page, and the next page is one more. Page numbers let the list at the front point at a page, and they let you stop reading and find your place again.
vocabulary

corner: the spot where two edges of a page meet.
place: the spot you stopped at.
connection
Describe the connection between page numbers and the list at the front.
Page numbers let a list at the front point at a page.
note: Best done with a real book open. Ask the child to find page nine two ways: by turning, and by using the list.

title: What the Picture Shows

p: The words say the bird has a long bill.
The picture shows you just how long that bill is.
The words do not say what color the bird is.
But the picture shows that the bird is bright blue.
So both parts of the page tell you different things.
The words say the bird has a long bill.
The picture shows how long it is.
The words do not say the color.
The picture shows it is bright blue.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the picture tell you that the words do not?
The picture shows that the bird is bright blue.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. how long the bill is) and paragraph D (i.e. the color).
summarize
Tell what the words do and what the picture does.

The words say the bird has a long bill and the picture shows just how long. The words do not say the color, but the picture shows the bird is bright blue. Both parts of the page tell you different things.
vocabulary

bill: the hard mouth of a bird.
color: red, blue, green and the rest.
connection
Describe the connection between the words and the picture on this page.
Both parts of the page tell you different things, because the words give the long bill and the picture gives the bright blue.
note: Cover the picture, read the words, and ask what the child still does not know. Then uncover it. That is the whole standard in one move.

title: The Words Say More

p: The photo shows a big bear standing in a river.
You can see its fur, its claws and the water.
The photo cannot tell you that the bear is hungry.
It cannot tell you the fish come here every fall.
The words have to say those things for you.
The photo shows a bear in a river.
You can see its fur and the water.
The photo cannot say the bear is hungry.
It cannot say when the fish come.

qs: main idea/detail
What can you see in the photo?
You can see its fur, its claws and the water.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. hungry) and paragraph D (i.e. when the fish come).
summarize
Tell what the photo shows and what it cannot.

The photo shows a big bear standing in a river, and you can see its fur, its claws and the water. It cannot tell you the bear is hungry or that the fish come every fall, so the words have to say those things.
vocabulary

photo: a picture made with a camera.
claws: the sharp hard nails on an animal's foot.
connection
Describe the connection between what a photo cannot show and the words.
The photo cannot tell you that the bear is hungry or when the fish come, so the words have to say those things for you.
note: This is the other half of the standard from What the Picture Shows. Read the two together if you can.

title: A Picture of a Beak

p: The page shows two different birds side by side.
One beak is thin and sharp, like a needle.
The other beak is wide and flat, like a spoon.
The words say the thin one drinks from deep flowers.
Together the picture and the words tell you why it is shaped that way.
The page shows two birds side by side.
One beak is thin like a needle.
The other beak is wide and flat.
The words say the thin one drinks from flowers.

qs: main idea/detail
What are the two beaks like?
One beak is thin and sharp, like a needle, and the other is wide and flat, like a spoon.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the thin beak) and paragraph D (i.e. what the words add).
summarize
Tell what the page shows about beaks.

The page shows two birds side by side. One beak is thin and sharp like a needle, and the other is wide and flat like a spoon. The words say the thin one drinks from deep flowers, so the picture and the words together tell you why it is shaped that way.
vocabulary

beak: the hard mouth of a bird.
needle: a thin sharp tool for sewing.
connection
Describe the connection between the shape of the beak and what the bird eats.
The words say the thin one drinks from deep flowers, and the picture shows that beak is thin and sharp like a needle.
note: Shape and job is the big idea underneath. Ask what the wide flat beak might be for before the child reads anything else.

title: The Map and the Words

p: A map of the zoo shows where each animal lives.
You can see that the lions are near the gate.
The map cannot tell you when the lions are fed.
The words under the map say feeding is at two.
You need both to plan your day at the zoo.
A zoo map shows where each animal lives.
You can see the lions near the gate.
The map cannot say when they are fed.
The words say feeding is at two.
You need both to plan your day.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the map show you?
A map of the zoo shows where each animal lives, and you can see that the lions are near the gate.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. what the map cannot say) and paragraph D (i.e. the words under it).
summarize
Tell what the map does and what the words do.

The zoo map shows where each animal lives, so you can see the lions near the gate. The map cannot tell you when the lions are fed, but the words under it say feeding is at two, so you need both to plan your day.
vocabulary

map: a picture that shows where things are.
feeding: the time an animal is given food.
connection
Describe the connection between the map and the words under it.
The map shows where the lions are and the words say feeding is at two, so you need both to plan your day at the zoo.
note: Where and when is a clean split for this age. Ask which question the map answers and which one the words answer.

title: What a Photo Cannot Tell You

p: A photo shows a volcano with gray smoke above it.
You can see the gray smoke and the dark rock.
A photo cannot tell you how hot that rock is.
It cannot tell you the smoke smells like old eggs.
Only words can tell you both of those things.
A photo shows a volcano with smoke.
You can see the smoke and the rock.
A photo cannot say how hot it is.
It cannot say what the smoke smells like.
Only words can tell you that.

qs: main idea/detail
What can you see in the photo?
You can see the gray smoke and the dark rock.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. how hot) and paragraph D (i.e. the smell).
summarize
Tell what a photo can show and what it cannot.
A photo of a volcano shows the gray smoke and the dark rock. It cannot tell you how hot the rock is or that the smoke smells like old eggs, so only words can tell you those things.
vocabulary

volcano: a mountain that can push out hot rock and smoke.
smells: what your nose tells you about something.
connection
Describe the connection between what you cannot see and what words do.
A photo cannot tell you how hot the rock is or what the smoke smells like, so only words can tell you both of those things.
note: Heat and smell are the two things no picture carries. That is a rule a child can take to every book on the shelf.

title: The Big Picture of a Farm

p: One wide picture shows the whole farm at one time.
The red barn sits close to the road in front.
A big field of corn grows behind the barn.
A small pond sits at the far end of the field.
The picture shows how all of the parts fit together.
One wide picture shows the whole farm.
The red barn is near the road.
A field of corn grows behind the barn.
A small pond sits at the far end.
The picture shows how the parts fit.

qs: main idea/detail
What is behind the barn?
A big field of corn grows behind the barn.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. the pond) and paragraph E (i.e. the parts fitting together).
summarize
Tell what the picture of the farm shows.

One wide picture shows the whole farm at one time. The red barn sits close to the road, a field of corn grows behind it, and a small pond sits at the far end. The picture shows how all the parts fit together.
vocabulary

barn: the big building on a farm.
pond: a small body of still water.
connection
Describe the connection between the wide picture and knowing where things are.
One wide picture shows the whole farm at one time, so it shows how all of the parts fit together.
note: Have the child describe the farm with the picture covered. Then uncover it and ask what they could not have said.

title: Steps in a Picture

p: Four small pictures show you how to wash a big dog.
In picture one the dog stands in the tub.
In picture two the soap goes on its back.
In picture three the water rinses all the soap off.
The numbers tell you which picture comes first and last.
Four pictures show how to wash a dog.
In picture one the dog is in the tub.
In picture two the soap goes on.
In picture three the water rinses it off.
The numbers tell you what comes first.

qs: main idea/detail
What happens in picture two?
In picture two the soap goes on its back.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. picture one) and paragraph E (i.e. the numbers).
summarize
Tell how the pictures show washing a dog.

Four small pictures show how to wash a dog. In picture one the dog stands in the tub, in picture two the soap goes on, and in picture three the water rinses it off. The numbers tell you which picture comes first.
vocabulary

rinse: to wash soap off with clean water.
tub: the big bowl you wash in.
connection
Describe the connection between the numbers and the order.
The numbers tell you which picture comes first and last, so you know the soap goes on before the water rinses it off.
note: Hide the numbers and shuffle the steps. The child will see fast what the numbers were doing.

title: Follow the Arrow

p: A picture of a plant has three arrows drawn on it.
One arrow points down from the cloud to the leaf.
One arrow points from the soil up through the stem.
The last arrow points back out of the leaf.
Together the arrows show the way the water travels.
A plant picture has three arrows on it.
One arrow points from the cloud to the leaf.
One points from the soil up the stem.
The last points out of the leaf.
The arrows show where the water goes.

qs: main idea/detail
How many arrows are on the picture?
A picture of a plant has three arrows drawn on it.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the arrow from the soil) and paragraph E (i.e. what the arrows show).
summarize
Tell what the arrows on the plant picture show.

A plant picture has three arrows. One points down from the cloud to the leaf, one points from the soil up through the stem, and the last points back out of the leaf. Together they show the way the water travels.
vocabulary

arrow: a mark that points the way.
stem: the part of a plant that holds it up.
connection
Describe the connection between the three arrows.
Together the arrows show the way the water travels, from the cloud to the leaf, from the soil up the stem, and back out of the leaf.
note: An arrow means direction, and children read it as decoration. Trace each one with a finger before talking about it.

title: A Picture with Labels

p: A picture of a bee has small words beside it.
A thin line runs from each word to one part.
One word says wing, and its line goes to a wing.
Those small words beside a picture are called labels.
Labels let a picture teach you the name of each part.
A bee picture has small words beside it.
A line runs from each word to a part.
One word says wing and points to the wing.
Labels teach you the name of each part.

qs: main idea/detail
What are the small words called?
Those small words beside a picture are called labels.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the lines) and paragraph E (i.e. what labels do).
summarize
Tell what labels do on a picture.

A picture of a bee has small words beside it, and a thin line runs from each word to one part. One word says wing and its line goes to a wing. Those words are called labels, and they let a picture teach you the name of each part.
vocabulary

label: a small word beside a picture that names a part.
wing: the part a bee flies with.
connection
Describe the connection between the line and the label.
A thin line runs from each word to one part, so the word wing goes with the wing and not with something else.
note: The line is the part children ignore, and it is the part that makes a label a label. Ask what would happen without the lines.

title: The Picture at the Start

p: A big picture sits at the start of this part.
It shows a town street covered in deep snow.
No cars are moving and one shop is dark inside.
Before you read a word, you know the storm was big.
The picture gets your head ready for the words.
A big picture is at the start of this part.
It shows a street covered in deep snow.
No cars move and one shop is dark.
Before you read, you know the storm was big.
The picture gets you ready for the words.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the picture show?
It shows a town street covered in deep snow.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. knowing before you read) and paragraph E (i.e. getting ready).
summarize
Tell what the picture at the start does.

A big picture at the start of the part shows a town street covered in deep snow, with no cars moving and one shop dark. Before you read a word you know the storm was big, so the picture gets your head ready for the words.
vocabulary

storm: strong wind, rain or snow.
ready: set to begin.
connection
Describe the connection between the picture and the words that come after it.
Before you read a word, the picture tells you the storm was big, so it gets your head ready for the words.
note: Ask the child to predict one thing the words will say. Then read and check. That is the habit this article is building.

title: Three Reasons to Wash Your Hands

p: You should always wash your hands before you eat.
First, germs on your hands can get on your food.
Second, germs you cannot see can still make you sick.
Third, soap and water take the germs right off.
Those three reasons are why the sink is by the door.
Wash your hands before you eat.
First, germs can get on your food.
Second, germs can make you sick.
Third, soap takes the germs off.
That is why the sink is by the door.

qs: main idea/detail
What is the third reason?
Third, soap and water take the germs right off.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. germs on food) and paragraph D (i.e. what soap does).
summarize
Tell the three reasons to wash your hands.
Germs on your hands can get on your food, germs you cannot see can still make you sick, and soap and water take the germs right off. Those three reasons are why the sink is by the door.
vocabulary

germ: a tiny living thing that can make you sick.
reason: why somebody thinks something is true.
connection
Describe the connection between germs you cannot see and washing anyway.
Germs you cannot see can still make you sick, so soap and water take them right off even when your hands look clean.
note: The words first, second and third are doing the work of RI.1.8. Have the child count the reasons on their fingers.

title: Why Plants Need Sun

p: A plant left in a dark closet will not grow well.
One reason is that leaves make food out of light.
Another reason is that light keeps the stem strong.
A plant with no light grows pale and floppy.
The book gives both of those reasons on one page.
A plant in a dark closet will not grow.
One reason is that leaves make food from light.
Another reason is that light keeps the stem strong.
A plant with no light grows pale.

qs: main idea/detail
What is one reason a plant needs light?
One reason is that leaves make food out of light.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the strong stem) and paragraph D (i.e. pale and floppy).
summarize
Tell why a plant needs sun.
A plant in a dark closet will not grow well. One reason is that leaves make food out of light, and another is that light keeps the stem strong. A plant with no light grows pale and floppy.
vocabulary

pale: having less color than usual.
floppy: too soft to stand up.
connection
Describe the connection between the two reasons and the floppy plant.
Leaves make food out of light and light keeps the stem strong, so a plant with no light grows pale and floppy.
note: Two reasons, and paragraph D is the proof for both. Ask which paragraph tells you what happens without sun.

title: Why We Practice the Fire Drill

p: Our class practices a fire drill four times a year.
One reason is that we learn the way out by heart.
Another reason is that nobody has to think in a hurry.
A third reason is that the teacher can count us fast.
Practice turns a scary thing into a plan we know.
Our class practices a fire drill four times a year.
One reason is we learn the way out.
Another is that nobody has to think fast.
A third is that the teacher can count us.
Practice makes it a plan we know.

qs: main idea/detail
How many times a year does the class practice?
Our class practices a fire drill four times a year.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. learning the way out) and paragraph D (i.e. counting).
summarize
Tell why the class practices a fire drill.

The class practices four times a year so they learn the way out by heart, so nobody has to think in a hurry, and so the teacher can count them fast. Practice turns a scary thing into a plan they know.
vocabulary

drill: practice for something that might happen.
by heart: known so well you do not have to think.
connection
Describe the connection between practicing and not having to think.
Practicing four times a year means the class learns the way out by heart, so nobody has to think in a hurry.
note: Paragraph E is the author's point and B, C and D are the reasons. Ask the child which one is the point.

title: Why Bats Help Us

p: Some people are scared of bats, but bats help us.
One reason is that a bat eats many bugs each night.
Another reason is that some bats carry pollen to flowers.
A third reason is that bat droppings make good soil.
The writer gives three reasons to leave bats alone.
Some people fear bats, but bats help us.
One reason is a bat eats many bugs.
Another is that bats carry pollen to flowers.
A third is that their droppings make good soil.

qs: main idea/detail
What does a bat eat?
One reason is that a bat eats many bugs each night.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. pollen) and paragraph E (i.e. three reasons).
summarize
Tell why bats help us.
A bat eats many bugs each night, some bats carry pollen to flowers, and bat droppings make good soil. The writer gives those three reasons to leave bats alone.
vocabulary

pollen: the yellow dust a flower makes.
droppings: the waste an animal leaves behind.
connection
Describe the connection between being scared of bats and the writer's reasons.
Some people are scared of bats, so the writer gives three reasons to leave bats alone.
note: The first sentence names what the writer is arguing against. Ask who the writer is talking to.

title: Why the Class Has Jobs

p: Every child in our class has a job for the week.
One reason is that the room gets tidy much faster.
Another reason is that everybody helps, not just one person.
A third reason is that each job teaches you something new.
The jobs change on Monday so everyone learns them all.
Every child in our class has a job.
One reason is the room gets tidy faster.
A third is that each job teaches you something.

qs: main idea/detail
When do the jobs change?
The jobs change on Monday so everyone learns them all.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. everybody helps) and paragraph E (i.e. changing on Monday).
summarize
Tell why the class has jobs.

Every child has a job for the week because the room gets tidy faster, because everybody helps instead of one person, and because each job teaches you something new. The jobs change on Monday so everyone learns them all.
vocabulary

tidy: neat and put away.
job: work that is yours to do.
connection
Describe the connection between changing the jobs and learning them all.
The jobs change on Monday so everyone learns them all, instead of one child doing the same job every week.
note: Paragraph E answers a question the reasons raise. Ask what would happen if the jobs never changed.

title: Two Pages About Bees

p: Both of these pages are about the same bee.
The first page tells how a bee makes sweet honey.
The second page tells how and why a bee stings.
Both pages say that a bee lives in a hive.
Only the second page says a bee can sting once.
The first page tells how a bee makes honey.
The second page tells how a bee stings.
Both pages say a bee lives in a hive.
Only the second says a bee stings once.

qs: main idea/detail
What do both pages say?
Both pages say that a bee lives in a hive.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. honey) and paragraph C (i.e. stinging).
summarize
Tell how the two pages are alike and different.
Both pages are about bees and both say a bee lives in a hive. The first page tells how a bee makes honey and the second tells how a bee stings, and only the second says a bee can sting once.
vocabulary

hive: the home a group of bees shares.
sting: to push a sharp point into skin.
connection
Describe the connection between the two pages.
Both pages are about the same bee and both say it lives in a hive, but one is about honey and the other is about stinging.
note: Same and different is the whole standard. Make two columns and fill them in as you read.

title: Two Books About Night

p: Both books tell what happens after the sun goes down.
One book is about owls that hunt in the dark.
The other book is about the stars that come out.
Both books say the air gets cooler at night.
The owl book has photos and the star book has maps.
Both books tell what happens after the sun goes down.
One book is about owls hunting.
The other is about stars coming out.
Both say the air gets cooler.
One has photos and one has maps.

qs: main idea/detail
What do both books say?
Both books say the air gets cooler at night.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the owls) and paragraph E (i.e. photos and maps).
summarize
Tell how the two books are alike and different.

Both books are about what happens after the sun goes down and both say the air gets cooler. One is about owls that hunt in the dark and the other is about the stars, and the owl book has photos while the star book has maps.
vocabulary

hunt: to look for food to catch.
map: a picture that shows where things are.
connection
Describe the connection between the topic and the pictures each book uses.
The owl book has photos and the star book has maps, because one shows an animal you can see and one shows where things are in the sky.
note: Paragraph E compares the pictures, not the words, which is a step up. Ask why a star book would want a map.

title: Two Books About Puddles

p: Both of these books have a puddle on the cover.
One book shows how a puddle dries up in the sun.
The other book shows what can live inside a puddle.
Both books say a puddle starts with rain.
Only one of them names the bugs in the water.
Both books have a puddle on the cover.
One book shows how a puddle dries.
The other shows what lives in a puddle.
Both say a puddle starts with rain.
Only one names the bugs in the water.

qs: main idea/detail
What do both books say?
Both books say a puddle starts with rain.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. drying) and paragraph C (i.e. what lives there).
summarize
Tell how the two puddle books are alike and different.
Both have a puddle on the cover and both say a puddle starts with rain. One shows how a puddle dries in the sun and the other shows what can live inside a puddle, and only one of them names the bugs.
vocabulary

cover: the outside front of a book.
dries: loses its water.
connection
Describe the connection between the two books.
Both books say a puddle starts with rain, but one follows the water out and the other looks at what lives in it.
note: Same start, two directions. Ask the child which book they would pick to answer a question about mosquitoes.

title: Two Books About Frogs

p: Both books are about frogs and both are true.
One book follows an egg until it becomes a frog.
The other book shows frogs from all over the world.
Both books say a frog starts life in water.
The world book has a map and the egg book does not.
One follows an egg until it is a frog.
The other shows frogs from many places.
Both say a frog starts life in water.

qs: main idea/detail
What do both books say?
Both books say a frog starts life in water.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the egg) and paragraph E (i.e. the map).
summarize
Tell how the two frog books are alike and different.

Both are about frogs and both say a frog starts life in water. One follows an egg until it becomes a frog, and the other shows frogs from all over the world. The world book has a map and the egg book does not.
vocabulary

egg: what a frog hatches from.
world: all the places on Earth.
connection
Describe the connection between what each book is about and whether it has a map.
The world book has a map because it shows frogs from all over, and the egg book does not need one because it follows just one frog.
note: Paragraph E is a reason hiding inside a comparison. Ask the child why one book needs a map and the other does not.

title: Two Books About Snow

p: Both of these books are about snow in winter.
One book shows how a single snowflake is made in a cloud.
The other book shows how a town clears its roads.
Both books say that snow is water that froze.
One book is mostly pictures and one is mostly words.
One shows how a snowflake is made.
The other shows how a town clears roads.
Both say snow is water that froze.
One is mostly pictures and one is mostly words.

qs: main idea/detail
What do both books say?
Both books say that snow is water that froze.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. clearing roads) and paragraph E (i.e. pictures and words).
summarize
Tell how the two snow books are alike and different.

Both are about snow in winter and both say snow is water that froze. One shows how a snowflake is made in a cloud and the other shows how a town clears its roads, and one book is mostly pictures while the other is mostly words.
vocabulary

snowflake: one small piece of falling snow.
clears: takes away so a road is open.
connection
Describe the connection between the two books' topics.
Both books say snow is water that froze, but one is about how it forms and the other is about what people do once it lands.
note: One book is about nature and one about people, on the same topic. That split is worth naming out loud.

title: How a Turtle Hides

p: A turtle carries its own hard house on its back.
When something scares it, the turtle pulls its head in.
Its legs fold in behind strong plates of shell.
A hungry bird can peck the shell and get nothing.
When the bird gives up, the turtle just walks away.
A turtle carries its house on its back.
When it is scared, it pulls its head in.
Its legs fold in behind the shell.
A bird can peck the shell and get nothing.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the turtle pull in first?
When something scares it, the turtle pulls its head in.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the legs) and paragraph D (i.e. the bird pecking).
summarize
Tell how a turtle hides.

A turtle carries a hard house on its back. When something scares it, it pulls its head in and folds its legs behind strong plates of shell. A hungry bird can peck the shell and get nothing, and when the bird gives up the turtle walks away.
vocabulary

shell: the hard cover on a turtle's back.
peck: to hit with a beak.
connection
Describe the connection between the shell and the bird giving up.
A hungry bird can peck the shell and get nothing, so the bird gives up and the turtle walks away.
note: Nothing happens in paragraph D, and that is the point. Ask what the turtle did to win.

title: The Ice Cream Truck

p: The ice cream truck plays the same song every day.
The song tells you the truck is close before you see it.
The driver keeps the freezer running the whole time.
If the freezer stops, the ice cream turns to soup.
That is why the truck never parks for long.
The ice cream truck plays the same song.
The song tells you the truck is close.
The driver keeps the freezer running.
If it stops, the ice cream melts.
That is why the truck does not park long.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the song tell you?
The song tells you the truck is close before you see it.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the freezer) and paragraph E (i.e. not parking long).
summarize
Tell how an ice cream truck works.

The truck plays the same song every day, which tells you it is close before you see it. The driver keeps the freezer running the whole time, because if it stops the ice cream turns to soup, and that is why the truck never parks for long.
vocabulary

freezer: a cold box that keeps things frozen.
parks: stops and stays in one place.
connection
Describe the connection between the freezer and how long the truck stays.
If the freezer stops the ice cream turns to soup, which is why the truck never parks for long.
note: The sound comes before the sight, and children know this from life. Start there and the rest follows.

title: Why Leaves Have Veins

p: Hold a leaf up to the light and look closely.
Thin lines run from the stem out to the edges.
Those lines are tubes that carry water through the leaf.
They also hold the flat part of the leaf open.
A leaf with broken veins goes limp and dries out.
Hold a leaf up to the light.
Thin lines run from the stem to the edges.
Those lines carry water through the leaf.
They also hold the leaf open and flat.
A leaf with broken lines dries out.

qs: main idea/detail
What do the thin lines carry?
Those lines are tubes that carry water through the leaf.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. holding the leaf open) and paragraph E (i.e. a broken leaf).
summarize
Tell what the veins in a leaf do.
Thin lines run from the stem out to the edges of a leaf. They are tubes that carry water through the leaf, and they also hold the flat part open. A leaf with broken veins goes limp and dries out.
vocabulary

vein: a thin tube in a leaf that carries water.
limp: soft and drooping.
connection
Describe the connection between the veins and the leaf staying flat.
The veins hold the flat part of the leaf open, so a leaf with broken veins goes limp and dries out.
note: Two jobs for one part, which is a useful idea early. Hold a real leaf to a window while you read paragraph A.

title: The Bus Driver's Mirror

p: A school bus has a long wide mirror above the driver.
The mirror lets her see every row without turning around.
She checks it once before she lets the bus move.
She checks it again each time the door opens.
The mirror is how one adult watches fifty children.
A school bus has a long mirror above the driver.
The mirror lets her see every row.
She checks it before the bus moves.
She checks it each time the door opens.
One adult can watch fifty children.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the mirror let the driver see?
The mirror lets her see every row without turning around.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. before the bus moves) and paragraph E (i.e. one adult and fifty children).
summarize
Tell what the bus driver's mirror is for.

A school bus has a long mirror above the driver that lets her see every row without turning around. She checks it before the bus moves and again each time the door opens, which is how one adult watches fifty children.
vocabulary

mirror: glass that shows what is behind you.
row: a line of seats side by side.
connection
Describe the connection between the mirror and the driver not turning around.
The mirror lets her see every row without turning around, so she can watch the children and the road at once.
note: Paragraph E is the point and it is a number. Ask how else one person could watch fifty.

title: How a Zipper Works

p: A zipper has two rows of small metal teeth.
The slider pulls the two rows together as it goes up.
Each tooth hooks into the gap beside the one across.
Pulling the slider down unhooks them again in order.
A zipper that catches has one tooth out of line.
A zipper has two rows of small teeth.
The slider pulls the rows together.
Each tooth hooks beside the one across.
A stuck zipper has one tooth out of line.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the slider do?
The slider pulls the two rows together as it goes up.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. hooking) and paragraph E (i.e. a zipper that catches).
summarize
Tell how a zipper works.

A zipper has two rows of small metal teeth. The slider pulls the rows together as it goes up, and each tooth hooks into the gap beside the one across. Pulling the slider down unhooks them in order, and a zipper that catches has one tooth out of line.
vocabulary

slider: the part you pull on a zipper.
teeth: the small metal pieces that hook together.
connection
Describe the connection between the teeth and a zipper that catches.
Each tooth hooks into the gap beside the one across, so a zipper that catches has one tooth out of line.
note: Children can test paragraph E on their own coat. Look for the one tooth that is bent.
